title: A Saturday at the library
text:
{土曜日|どようび}、{私|わたし}は{図書館|としょかん}に{行|い}きます。{図書館|としょかん}は{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くにあります。{家|いえ}から{歩|ある}いて{十分|じゅっぷん}です。

{朝|あさ}は{人|ひと}が{少|すく}ないです。{私|わたし}は{九時|くじ}に{行|い}きます。{日本語|にほんご}の{本|ほん}を{読|よ}みます。{十二時|じゅうにじ}に{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}ります。
translation: On Saturdays, I go to the library. The library is near the station. It is a ten-minute walk from home. There are few people in the morning. I go at nine. I read Japanese books. I return home at twelve.

questions.prompt: Where is the library?
choices: Near the station
Inside a school
Far from the town
Next to a hospital
questions.explanation: The passage says 図書館は駅の近くにあります: the library is near the station.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator get there?
choices: By walking for ten minutes
By taking a train for ten minutes
By riding a bus for an hour
By driving with a friend
questions.explanation: 家から歩いて十分です means it is a ten-minute walk from home.

questions.prompt: Why is the morning a good time to visit?
choices: There are fewer people
All books are free to keep
The library closes at nine
Friends meet there every morning
questions.explanation: 朝は人が少ないです says there are few people in the morning.

title: Shopping for lunch
text:
{今日|きょう}は{日曜日|にちようび}です。{父|ちち}とスーパーに{行|い}きます。{昼|ひる}ご{飯|はん}にカレーを{作|つく}ります。{家|いえ}に{肉|にく}があります。でも、{野菜|やさい}はありません。

スーパーで、じゃがいもとにんじんを{買|か}います。{父|ちち}は{牛乳|ぎゅうにゅう}も{買|か}います。{買|か}い{物|もの}は{全部|ぜんぶ}で{千円|せんえん}です。{家|いえ}で{一緒|いっしょ}にカレーを{作|つく}ります。
translation: Today is Sunday. I go to the supermarket with my father. We will make curry for lunch. There is meat at home, but there are no vegetables. At the supermarket, we buy potatoes and carrots. My father also buys milk. The shopping costs one thousand yen in total. At home, we make curry together.

questions.prompt: What will they make for lunch?
choices: Curry
Sushi
Sandwiches
Noodles
questions.explanation: 昼ご飯にカレーを作ります explicitly states that lunch will be curry.

questions.prompt: Why do they need to buy vegetables?
choices: There are none at home
Their father dislikes meat
The shop has no milk
They are cooking for a restaurant
questions.explanation: 家に肉があります。でも、野菜はありません contrasts the meat they have with the vegetables they lack.

questions.prompt: How much does all the shopping cost?
choices: 100 yen
questions.explanation: 買い物は全部で千円です gives the total as one thousand yen.

title: The umbrella left behind
text:
{昨日|きのう}、{仕事|しごと}が{終|お}わってから、{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くの{喫茶店|きっさてん}で{友達|ともだち}に{会|あ}いました。{店|みせ}に{入|はい}るときは{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}っていましたが、{帰|かえ}るときはやんでいました。

{今朝|けさ}、かさがないことに{気|き}がつきました。{喫茶店|きっさてん}に{電話|でんわ}すると、{店|みせ}の{人|ひと}が「{青|あお}いかさを{預|あず}かっています」と{言|い}いました。{私|わたし}のかさも{青|あお}いので、{仕事|しごと}の{後|あと}で{取|と}りに{行|い}くことにしました。{店|みせ}の{人|ひと}にお{礼|れい}を{言|い}いたいです。
translation: Yesterday, after work, I met a friend at a café near the station. It was raining when I entered, but it had stopped when I left. This morning, I noticed my umbrella was missing. I called the café, and a staff member said they were keeping a blue umbrella. Mine is blue too, so I decided to go and collect it after work. I want to thank the staff member.

questions.prompt: When did the narrator notice the umbrella was missing?
choices: This morning
On entering the café
During yesterday's lunch
After collecting it
questions.explanation: 今朝、かさがないことに気がつきました places the discovery this morning.

questions.prompt: What suggests the umbrella at the café belongs to the narrator?
choices: It is blue, like the narrator's umbrella
It has the narrator's phone number
A friend bought it that morning
The café only keeps black umbrellas
questions.explanation: The staff describe a blue umbrella, and the narrator says 私のかさも青い.

questions.prompt: What will the narrator do after work?
choices: Collect the umbrella from the café
Buy a new umbrella at the station
Ask a friend to phone the café
Wait at home for a delivery
questions.explanation: 仕事の後で取りに行くことにしました means the narrator decided to go and get it after work.

title: A small vegetable garden
text:
{春|はる}から、{近所|きんじょ}の{人|ひと}たちと{小|ちい}さな{畑|はたけ}で{野菜|やさい}を{育|そだ}てています。{初|はじ}めは{何|なに}も{分|わ}からなかったので、{年上|としうえ}の{人|ひと}に{教|おし}えてもらいました。

{毎日|まいにち}{行|い}くことはできませんが、{土曜日|どようび}の{朝|あさ}は{必ず|かならず}{水|みず}をやります。{先週|せんしゅう}、{初|はじ}めてトマトが{赤|あか}くなりました。{店|みせ}で{買|か}うトマトより{少|すこ}し{小|ちい}さかったですが、とてもおいしかったです。{来年|らいねん}は、{子供|こども}と{一緒|いっしょ}に{育|そだ}ててみたいです。
translation: Since spring, I have been growing vegetables in a small garden with people in the neighborhood. At first I knew nothing, so older neighbors taught me. I cannot go every day, but I always water the plants on Saturday mornings. Last week, a tomato turned red for the first time. It was a little smaller than tomatoes from the shop, but delicious. Next year, I would like to try growing vegetables with my child.

questions.prompt: How did the narrator learn to grow vegetables?
choices: Older neighbors taught them
They had worked on a farm for years
Their child taught them everything
They learned only from television
questions.explanation: 年上の人に教えてもらいました says the narrator received instruction from older people.

questions.prompt: When does the narrator always water the plants?
choices: Saturday morning
Every evening
Sunday night
Only when it rains
questions.explanation: 土曜日の朝は必ず水をやります specifies Saturday mornings.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator want to try next year?
choices: Growing vegetables with their child
Selling the entire garden
Buying all vegetables from a shop
Stopping the Saturday visits
questions.explanation: The final sentence expresses a wish to grow vegetables with the narrator's child next year.

title: Bicycles near the station
text:
{駅前|えきまえ}では、{歩道|ほどう}に{置|お}かれた{自転車|じてんしゃ}が{問題|もんだい}になっていた。{市|し}は{新|あたら}しい{駐輪場|ちゅうりんじょう}を{作|つく}ったが、{利用|りよう}する{人|ひと}は{思|おも}ったほど{増|ふ}えなかった。{入口|いりぐち}が{駅|えき}と{反対側|はんたいがわ}にあり、{遠回|とおまわ}りしなければならなかったからだ。

そこで{市|し}は、{利用者|りようしゃ}の{意見|いけん}を{聞|き}き、{駅|えき}に{近|ちか}い{場所|ばしょ}にも{入口|いりぐち}を{設|もう}けた。{案内|あんない}の{看板|かんばん}も{増|ふ}やしたところ、{利用者|りようしゃ}が{少|すこ}しずつ{増|ふ}えてきた。{施設|しせつ}を{作|つく}るだけでなく、{使|つか}う{人|ひと}の{立場|たちば}で{考|かんが}えることが{大切|たいせつ}なのだ。
translation: Bicycles left on the sidewalks near the station had become a problem. The city built a new bicycle parking facility, but use did not rise as much as expected. Its entrance was on the side away from the station, requiring a detour. The city listened to users and added an entrance closer to the station. After it added more signs too, use began to increase gradually. Building a facility is not enough; considering the user's perspective matters.

questions.prompt: Why did few people initially use the new parking area?
choices: The entrance required an inconvenient detour
Bicycles were prohibited inside
It opened only on Saturdays
It had no space for bicycles
questions.explanation: The text links low use to the entrance being on the opposite side, forcing users to take a detour.

questions.prompt: What did the city change after hearing users' opinions?
choices: It added an entrance near the station and more signs
It closed the station entrance permanently
It charged more for parking on the sidewalk
It removed all signs near the facility
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes a new nearby entrance and additional guidance signs.

questions.prompt: What is the main lesson of the passage?
choices: Facilities should be designed from users' perspectives
New construction always solves a problem immediately
Signs are more important than every other feature
People should stop using bicycles entirely
questions.explanation: The final sentence emphasizes 使う人の立場で考える: thinking from the perspective of the people who use the facility.

title: An online study group
text:
{一人|ひとり}で{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}していたころは、{分|わ}からない{表現|ひょうげん}があると、すぐに{答|こた}えを{調|しら}べていた。しかし、それでは{自分|じぶん}の{考|かんが}えを{言葉|ことば}にする{練習|れんしゅう}が{足|た}りないと{感|かん}じた。

{今|いま}は、{週|しゅう}に{一度|いちど}、オンラインの{勉強会|べんきょうかい}に{参加|さんか}している。{参加者|さんかしゃ}は{短|みじか}い{記事|きじ}を{読|よ}み、まず{辞書|じしょ}を{使|つか}わずに{内容|ないよう}を{説明|せつめい}する。その{後|あと}で、お{互|たが}いに{質問|しつもん}したり、{表現|ひょうげん}を{確|たし}かめたりする。{間違|まちが}えることもあるが、{自分|じぶん}で{考|かんが}えてから{調|しら}べた{言葉|ことば}は、{前|まえ}より{覚|おぼ}えやすくなった。
translation: When I studied Japanese alone, I immediately looked up answers whenever I encountered an unfamiliar expression. But I felt this did not give me enough practice putting my thoughts into words. Now I attend an online study group once a week. Participants read a short article and first explain its content without a dictionary. Then they ask each other questions and check expressions. I make mistakes, but words I look up after thinking for myself are easier to remember than before.

questions.prompt: What was missing from the narrator's previous study method?
choices: Practice expressing their own thoughts
Access to any Japanese books
Enough time to look up answers
An internet connection at home
questions.explanation: The first paragraph identifies a lack of practice putting one's own thoughts into words.

questions.prompt: What do participants do before checking expressions?
choices: Explain an article without using a dictionary
Memorize the entire dictionary
Translate every word with an app
Take a formal examination
questions.explanation: まず辞書を使わずに内容を説明する describes their first activity.

questions.prompt: What change has the narrator noticed?
choices: Words checked after personal effort are easier to remember
They no longer make any mistakes
Studying alone has become unnecessary for everyone
Questions always prevent learning
questions.explanation: The last sentence says that thinking first and looking up words afterward has improved retention.

title: Reducing food waste
text:
あるスーパーでは、{消費期限|しょうひきげん}が{近|ちか}づいた{食品|しょくひん}を{割引|わりびき}するだけでなく、{家庭|かてい}で{使|つか}い{切|き}るための{献立|こんだて}も{紹介|しょうかい}している。{安|やす}さにつられて{必要以上|ひつよういじょう}に{買|か}えば、{店|みせ}での{廃棄|はいき}が{減|へ}っても、{家庭|かてい}で{捨|す}てる{量|りょう}が{増|ふ}えかねないからだ。

{店|みせ}は、{少人数|しょうにんずう}の{世帯|せたい}でも{買|か}いやすい{小分|こわ}けの{商品|しょうひん}を{増|ふ}やした。{包装|ほうそう}の{量|りょう}が{増|ふ}えるという{課題|かだい}はあるものの、{売|う}れ{残|のこ}りと{家庭|かてい}での{無駄|むだ}を{合|あ}わせて{減|へ}らすことを{目指|めざ}している。{食品|しょくひん}ロスへの{対策|たいさく}は、{一|ひと}つの{数字|すうじ}だけで{成果|せいか}を{判断|はんだん}せず、{流通|りゅうつう}から{食卓|しょくたく}までを{見渡|みわた}して{考|かんが}える{必要|ひつよう}がある。
translation: A supermarket not only discounts food approaching its use-by date but also suggests menus to help households use it up. If people buy more than necessary because it is cheap, household waste may rise even if store waste falls. The store has increased smaller packages suitable for small households. Although this increases packaging, the aim is to reduce both unsold stock and household waste. Food-waste measures should be judged across the chain from distribution to the dining table, not by one number alone.

questions.prompt: Why does the store suggest menus as well as discounts?
choices: To help customers use food rather than transfer waste into homes
To make all customers buy the largest packages
To avoid checking use-by dates
To stop households from cooking
questions.explanation: The store wants discounted food to be used up; buying too much can merely move waste from the store to the household.

questions.prompt: What trade-off accompanies smaller packages?
choices: They can reduce food waste while increasing packaging
They remove every environmental concern
They always increase both types of food waste
They prevent small households from shopping
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly acknowledges increased packaging as a challenge despite the intended reduction in wasted food.

questions.prompt: How does the author suggest evaluating these measures?
choices: Consider effects from distribution through household consumption
Use only the amount discarded by the store
Count packaging and ignore food entirely
Judge success solely by sales revenue
questions.explanation: The conclusion calls for a broad view from 流通 to 食卓, rather than relying on a single figure.

title: Flexibility and fair evaluation
text:
{在宅勤務|ざいたくきんむ}を{導入|どうにゅう}した{企業|きぎょう}で、{社員|しゃいん}の{満足度|まんぞくど}が{上|あ}がった。ところが、{制度|せいど}を{利用|りよう}する{社員|しゃいん}ほど、{評価|ひょうか}が{低|ひく}い{傾向|けいこう}も{見|み}られた。{成果|せいか}に{大|おお}きな{差|さ}はなくても、{上司|じょうし}と{顔|かお}を{合|あ}わせる{機会|きかい}が{少|すく}ないため、{働|はたら}きぶりが{伝|つた}わりにくかったのである。

{会社|かいしゃ}はこの{問題|もんだい}を{受|う}け、{出社|しゅっしゃ}している{時間|じかん}ではなく、{事前|じぜん}に{合意|ごうい}した{目標|もくひょう}と、その{達成|たっせい}までの{過程|かてい}を{確認|かくにん}する{方法|ほうほう}に{改|あらた}めた。{制度|せいど}を{設|もう}ければ{自動的|じどうてき}に{公平|こうへい}になるわけではない。{利用|りよう}した{人|ひと}が{不利|ふり}にならないよう、{評価|ひょうか}の{仕組|しく}みまで{見直|みなお}してこそ、{柔軟|じゅうなん}な{働|はたら}き{方|かた}が{実際|じっさい}の{選択肢|せんたくし}になる。
translation: At a company that introduced working from home, employee satisfaction rose. Yet employees using the scheme tended to receive lower evaluations. Even without major differences in results, less face-to-face contact with supervisors made their work harder to see. The company changed its method to assess agreed goals and the process of reaching them, rather than time in the office. Merely introducing a policy does not automatically create fairness. Flexible work becomes a real option only when evaluation systems are revised so that users are not disadvantaged.

questions.prompt: Why did remote workers tend to receive lower evaluations?
choices: Their contributions were less visible to supervisors
Their results were proven to be much worse
They refused all agreed goals
The scheme reduced satisfaction for everyone
questions.explanation: The text says results did not differ greatly, but fewer meetings with supervisors made employees' work less visible.

questions.prompt: What did the company decide to assess instead of office attendance?
choices: Agreed goals and the process of achieving them
Only the number of messages sent
Only the supervisor's first impression
The distance between home and the office
questions.explanation: 事前に合意した目標と、その達成までの過程 identifies both agreed goals and the path toward them.

questions.prompt: What is the author's central claim?
choices: Flexible policies need fair evaluation systems to become genuine options
Working from home must always be compulsory
Creating a policy alone guarantees fairness
Office attendance is the only reliable measure of work
questions.explanation: The conclusion argues that revising the evaluation system is necessary to prevent users of the policy from being disadvantaged.

title: What the numbers leave out
text:
{地域|ちいき}の{活性化|かっせいか}を{語|かた}る{際|さい}、{観光客数|かんこうきゃくすう}や{売上高|うりあげだか}が{成果|せいか}の{指標|しひょう}として{掲|かか}げられる。{比較|ひかく}しやすい{数字|すうじ}が{議論|ぎろん}を{助|たす}けることは{確|たし}かだ。しかし、{数値|すうち}の{上昇|じょうしょう}をもって、{住民|じゅうみん}の{暮|く}らしが{豊|ゆた}かになったと{断定|だんてい}することはできない。{来訪者|らいほうしゃ}の{増加|ぞうか}に{伴|ともな}って、{静|しず}かな{生活|せいかつ}や{日常|にちじょう}の{移動|いどう}のしやすさが{損|そこ}なわれる{場合|ばあい}もあるからだ。

だからといって、{測定|そくてい}そのものを{否定|ひてい}すべきだというのではない。{問|と}われるべきは、{何|なに}を{測|はか}り、{誰|だれ}の{経験|けいけん}を{見落|みお}としているのかである。{指標|しひょう}は{現実|げんじつ}を{理解|りかい}するための{手掛かり|てがかり}であって、{現実|げんじつ}そのものではない。{数値|すうち}に{表|あらわ}れにくい{声|こえ}を{聞|き}き{取|と}り、{必要|ひつよう}に{応|おう}じて{指標|しひょう}を{組|く}み{替|か}える{姿勢|しせい}があってこそ、{測定|そくてい}は{目的|もくてき}に{取|と}って{代|か}わることなく、{地域|ちいき}のために{機能|きのう}する。
translation: Tourist numbers and sales are often presented as measures of regional revitalization. Comparable numbers certainly help discussion. Yet an increase does not prove residents' lives have become richer: more visitors can undermine quiet living and convenient everyday travel. This is not an argument against measurement itself. We should ask what is being measured and whose experience is overlooked. Indicators are clues for understanding reality, not reality itself. Only by listening to voices that numbers miss and revising indicators when necessary can measurement serve the community without replacing the underlying purpose.

questions.prompt: What does the author dispute about higher tourist numbers?
choices: That they alone prove an improvement in residents' lives
That they can be counted at all
That they ever increase local sales
That they are relevant to any discussion
questions.explanation: The author accepts that figures help discussion but rejects treating rising figures as conclusive evidence of richer lives.

questions.prompt: What does 'indicators are clues, not reality itself' imply?
choices: Indicators provide a partial view that should be checked against lived experience
Indicators are always deliberately false
Only unmeasurable opinions deserve consideration
Every indicator should be replaced by tourist numbers
questions.explanation: The surrounding sentences ask whose experiences are overlooked and call for listening to voices not reflected in numbers.

questions.prompt: Which approach would the author most likely support?
choices: Revise metrics while consulting residents about overlooked effects
Maximize visitor totals regardless of local consequences
Abandon all measurement permanently
Retain existing metrics even when they distort priorities
questions.explanation: The conclusion supports listening, revising indicators, and keeping measurement subordinate to the community's actual purposes.

title: Convenience and the freedom to choose
text:
{動画|どうが}や{記事|きじ}を{勧|すす}める{仕組|しく}みは、{私|わたし}たちが{探|さが}す{手間|てま}を{省|はぶ}いてくれる。その{便利|べんり}さゆえに、{表示|ひょうじ}されたものの{中|なか}から{選|えら}ぶことを、{自分|じぶん}の{関心|かんしん}に{基|もと}づく{自由|じゆう}な{選択|せんたく}と{受|う}け{止|と}めがちだ。だが、{選択肢|せんたくし}がどのように{絞|しぼ}られたかが{見|み}えなければ、{選|えら}んだ{結果|けっか}だけから、その{自由|じゆう}の{程度|ていど}を{判断|はんだん}することはできない。

{未知|みち}の{分野|ぶんや}に{触|ふ}れる{機会|きかい}まで{減|へ}ってしまえば、{過去|かこ}の{好|この}みが{将来|しょうらい}の{関心|かんしん}を{狭|せば}めることにもなりかねない。{推薦|すいせん}を{一律|いちりつ}に{拒|こば}む{必要|ひつよう}はないが、その{理由|りゆう}を{確|たし}かめたり、あえて{別|べつ}の{経路|けいろ}で{探|さが}したりする{余地|よち}は{残|のこ}しておきたい。{便利|べんり}な{仕組|しく}みを{使|つか}いこなすとは、すべてを{任|まか}せることではなく、{任|まか}せる{範囲|はんい}を{自分|じぶん}で{選|えら}び{直|なお}せることであろう。
translation: Systems recommending videos and articles spare us the effort of searching. Their convenience encourages us to regard choosing among displayed items as a free choice based on our interests. Yet without seeing how the options were narrowed, we cannot judge that freedom from the chosen result alone. If exposure to unfamiliar fields also declines, past preferences may narrow future interests. There is no need to reject all recommendations, but we should retain room to examine their reasons and deliberately explore other routes. Mastering a convenient system means being able to reconsider what we entrust to it, rather than entrusting everything.

questions.prompt: Why is choosing from displayed recommendations not sufficient evidence of freedom?
choices: The process narrowing the available options may be hidden
The user never actually makes a selection
Every recommendation is chosen randomly
All recommended content is necessarily wrong
questions.explanation: The first paragraph distinguishes choosing a result from understanding how the choices were selected for display.

questions.prompt: What risk does the author identify in relying on past preferences?
choices: They may reduce exposure to unfamiliar fields and limit future interests
They guarantee a wider range of interests
They prevent systems from making any recommendations
They make every search take more time
questions.explanation: The text warns that fewer encounters with unfamiliar fields can let past preferences narrow future interests.

questions.prompt: What does the author mean by mastering a convenient system?
choices: Retaining the ability to decide and revise how much to delegate
Rejecting every automated recommendation without exception
Allowing the system to determine every future interest
Choosing only material that matches past behavior
questions.explanation: The final sentence defines effective use as being able to choose again the scope of what one leaves to the system.
